title: Onboarding Is More Than a Checklist
author: Will Thomas
summary: In this guest post for The Mindful Manager, executive coach Will Thomas argues that onboarding should go well beyond badges, desks and compliance videos. He opens with a new vice president who damaged relationships on his first day by announcing answers before understanding the culture. Drawing on the Society for Human Resource Management's four elements, compliance, clarification, culture and connection, he explains what a manager should add to the admin basics. Clarification means clear role expectations, 30/60/90-day goals and weekly one-on-ones, while culture means explaining unwritten rules and naming culture champions. Connection means deliberately introducing new hires to the people they need, and early wins, following Michael Watkins, give them a quick way to show value. He closes with reflective questions for managers about what they wish someone had done for them.
points: Skills only pay off if a new hire meshes with colleagues, so onboarding must teach culture, decision-making norms and trust-building as well as policies.
Compliance is the part nearly every company does; the differentiators are clarification, culture and connection.
Short 30/60/90-day goals and weekly one-on-ones keep new hires aligned without micromanaging them.
Managers should actively broker the new hire's network, giving names and reasons, because internal networks are a prerequisite for a good transition.
Assigning a small, independent early-win project builds credibility and focuses the hire's learning.
quotes: Coming in on the first day and announcing he had the answer to their problems is a bit like arriving at someone else’s house for the first time and telling them how to rearrange their furniture. You may have some good ideas, but it’s probably not going to go down well.

Organizations with a strong onboarding process improve new hire retention by 82% and productivity by over 70%. Companies with weak onboarding programs lose the confidence of their candidates and are more likely to lose these individuals in the first year.

Weekly one-on-ones with new hires shouldn’t be about micromanaging them, these sessions should be used to ensure they get your culture, understand what they’re doing and have the right level of support.
Just like you wouldn’t drive a car without knowing the traffic laws, you cannot perform well in an organization unless you know how people behave.
They need a network of “invisible lines” that complement the org chart’s solid lines and dotted lines, with trusting relationships that make them feel confident enough to contribute.
Suggest some projects they can do: low-hanging fruit that doesn’t require in-depth knowledge of the company, that has a positive impact, and that they can do on their own to demonstrate their skills.

Without it, people have to figure out what’s expected, how things work and how to build relationships by trial and error. That can create confusion for them and everyone around them, and undermine the investment you made to recruit them in the first place.
